task.title: Study Forensics: Randomized literacy program boosts children's reading
task.prompt: A large-scale study investigated a literacy support program in which elementary school students received weekly supplementary instruction over two school years. Students were randomly assigned to either the program or regular instruction. By the end of the first year, participants' reading proficiency was on average two and a half months ahead of the comparison group, and this advantage was still detectable 26 months later. The researchers note that the effect remained stable across all age groups and that no systematic disadvantages were observed.
task.context:
Randomized controlled trial with clear intervention-control comparison, long-term
follow-up, and cautious reporting. The agent should recognize it as solid without
hallucinating weaknesses.
task.reference_solution: A randomized controlled trial of a literacy program shows a 2.5-month reading advantage over controls that persists 26 months later. The study uses random assignment, reports measurable outcomes, and makes no overclaims. This is a clear solid case.

task.gold_justification:
The study was randomized, large-scale, and clearly compares intervention and control
groups. Results are reported as measurable gains in months of reading progress, and the
text remains cautious by only pointing to measured competency gains and their persistence.
A clear, robust case with no overclaim or mechanism gap.
task.curator_notes:
Imported from Dataset 6 (CaseE01). Originally German, translated to English for
consistency. Strong positive anchor for the solid category. Tests whether agents
correctly recognize clear improvements and cautious conclusions as solid without
hallucinating weaknesses. Based on Harvard CEPR MORE reading program research.

## Summary

This is a **solid study**. It is a randomized controlled trial in human subjects with appropriate controls, real-world outcomes (reading proficiency), and a reasonable follow-up period. The evidence tier (clinical_human RCT) directly supports the conclusion tier (human therapeutic benefit in literacy). Random assignment mitigates confounding, and the text appropriately bounds claims to the observed population and timeframe without overclaiming permanence or universality. No mechanism-vs-evidence gap, correlation-vs-causation error, or major confounding is apparent.

The main limitations are in the *reporting* (sample size, effect size in standardized units, and implementation details are not provided), not in the study design itself.
